Cardiology and hematology · published research

Cardiovascular aging

A long-term mouse study reported favorable changes in cardiac and vascular measures, gait symmetry, and survival in an accelerated-aging model. These are early findings from a genetically specific model, and their relevance to cardiovascular aging in people is unknown.

Evidence summary

What the evidence suggests

One long-term experiment found favorable changes in selected cardiac, vascular, gait, and survival outcomes in AC8 mice. The broader cardiovascular review discusses this same study, and no patient effect estimate is available.

Summary of the Evidence

In an accelerated-aging mouse model, near-infrared PBM was associated with improved cardiac measures, less aortic-wall stiffness, better gait symmetry, and higher survival in AC8 mice. Survival did not differ significantly in wild-type animals. Certainty for cardiovascular-aging outcomes or survival in people is very low (Syed et al. 2023).

Human and clinical evidence

No human study has tested PBM for cardiovascular aging. A 2023 review of cardiovascular PBM includes the same mouse study of age-associated remodeling, cardiac function, gait, and survival, but does not add a patient study or an independent cardiovascular-aging experiment (Ganipineni et al. 2023).

Animal evidence

The study treated 14-month-old AC8 transgenic mice and wild-type littermates with full-body near-infrared light or no treatment. During early treatment, the authors reported lower age-related increases in left-ventricular mass, lower end-diastolic volume in AC8 mice, higher ejection fraction, lower aortic-wall stiffness, and improved gait symmetry. Several effects persisted after the treatment pause. Cumulative survival was 100% in treated AC8 mice versus 43% in untreated AC8 mice, while survival did not significantly differ in wild-type mice (Syed et al. 2023).

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The experiment used full-body 850-nm near-infrared LED exposure at 25 mW/cm² for two minutes each weekday, with a reported fluence of 3 J/cm². The eight-month study period included 3.5 months of treatment, a three-month pause, and 1.5 months of resumed treatment. This is one regimen in a genetically altered model and does not identify an optimal dose or predict response in people (Syed et al. 2023).

Interpretation

One long-term mouse experiment reported favorable cardiac, vascular, gait, and survival findings in AC8 mice, with no significant survival difference in wild-type animals. A broader review discusses the same experiment rather than supplying independent replication. Effects on cardiovascular aging in people remain uncertain.

Certainty of evidence (estimate)

Very low for cardiovascular-aging outcomes or survival. Evidence comes from one accelerated-aging mouse experiment, with no patient study (Syed et al. 2023).

Rationale for the certainty assessment

Only one indication-specific experiment has examined cardiovascular aging, and it used genetically altered mice. The 2023 review’s discussion of aging relies on that same study, not a second experiment. The survival finding was confined to AC8 mice, with no significant difference in wild-type animals, and no human outcomes have been studied. Together, these limits leave very low certainty for outcomes in people (Syed et al. 2023; Ganipineni et al. 2023).
